title: He Was Banned From Every Gallery in Bucharest. His Front Room Became One Instead.
standfirst: Ion Țuculescu spent his working life studying pond mud at a Black Sea lake and his evenings painting the strange, undated final phase of his career. When the state refused him a hall in 1956, he opened his own apartment as a gallery instead — and the visitors' book that followed put his name beside Brâncuși's.

sections.heading: He Painted Watercolours to Cover the Train Fare to a Lake of Mud
sections.body: [Lake Techirghiol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Techirghiol) sits on Romania's Black Sea coast, a brackish stretch of water between the towns of Eforie and Techirghiol whose mud a local legend credits with curing a disabled man named Tekir. [Ion Țuculescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_%C8%9Auculescu) went there for years, not as a painter but as the biologist and physician he had trained to be — he graduated from both the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Bucharest's medical school by 1939, and biology, not medicine, became his real second career at the Romanian Academy. The trips weren't always funded. The physician Octavian Șerbănescu later testified that Țuculescu would paint watercolours purely to sell or trade for the [train fare down to the lake](https://www.observatorcultural.ro/articol/dincolo-de-dramatismul-naturist-al-lui-ion-tuculescu/). The research became a 525-page study of Techirghiol's mud, published by the Academy only after he died. What he spent those years looking at through a microscope is not incidental to what turns up a decade later in canvases like this one, made in the last and least documented stretch of his career.

sections.heading: The Catalogue Calls It Expressionism. He'd Left Recognisable Things Behind by Then.
sections.body: WikiArt files Blue Totem under Expressionism and gives it [no year at all](https://www.wikiart.org/en/ion-tuculescu/blue-totem) — a gap the record does nothing to close, since by the time this style of work was made Țuculescu had largely stopped dating things and stopped exhibiting. What lies between his early work and this one is decades, not a label's width. In Greece and Egypt in the early 1930s he was still painting representational scenes: ["I painted almost only sunny landscapes. I loved color"](https://academictraditions.com/artists/ion-tuculescu), he said of that period. From around 1942 he began pulling motifs from the woven scoarțe, the carpets, of his native Oltenia, replacing trees and clouds with their bark-like geometric patterning — what collectors now call his folkloric period. By the late 1950s those folk motifs had themselves dissolved into what one account calls ["pure electric discharges,"](https://academictraditions.com/artists/ion-tuculescu) fields with nothing representational left standing in them. Curators mounting a 2025 retrospective borrowed [his own word for these lurches](https://www.artsafari.ro/en/project/ion-tuculescu-en/): mutations. Later paintings put a single eye at the centre of otherwise abstract fields, a device the critic A. E. Baconsky [read as ancestral and totemic](https://tylercollection.omeka.net/items/show/784) — though a man who spent his working life at a lens might just as easily have been drawing it from a slide.

sections.heading: Locked Out of the Athenaeum, He Opened a Gallery in His Own Front Room
sections.body: By 1956 Țuculescu had held seven solo shows at the Romanian Athenaeum since his debut there in 1938. That year the [Union of Plastic Artists refused](https://romanialiterara.com/2020/05/ion-tuculescu-mai-putin-cunoscut/) him a hall for his new folkloric series, while, he believed, handing gallery space on Calea Victoriei to Ion Mirea, another physician-turned-painter he accused of lifting the same folk compositions. Rather than wait, Țuculescu opened an exhibition inside his own home, at [Strada Lizeanu no. 5](https://romanialiterara.com/2020/05/ion-tuculescu-mai-putin-cunoscut/), in October 1956 — the same month Hungary's uprising against Soviet rule began. Unauthorised and reviewed by no official paper, the show read, to the writers, painters and philosophers who came to see it, as a small act of defiance against a state that had already told him no.

sections.heading: The Guest Book Put Him Beside Brâncuși. The State Put Him Nowhere.
sections.body: Visitors signed a book on their way out of the Lizeanu apartment, and some of what they wrote survives. The painter Medi Dinu described being moved by walls "covered with pieces of painting as in peasant homes." The critic Vladimir Streinu wrote that the geometric carpet motifs, translated into the fantastic, amounted to "the new dimension of today's painting." The graphic artist Dragoș Morărescu went further, naming three names in one line: ["Brâncuși, Enescu, Țuculescu, cornerstones of truly Romanian art."](https://romanialiterara.com/2020/05/ion-tuculescu-mai-putin-cunoscut/) Among the other guests were the writers Geo Bogza, Gellu Naum and Nicolae Steinhardt. None of it changed anything officially. Țuculescu held no further solo exhibition for the rest of his life, appearing in just [three collective shows between 1957 and 1960](https://romanialiterara.com/2020/05/ion-tuculescu-mai-putin-cunoscut/). He died in Bucharest on 27 July 1962, at fifty-two, and was buried at Cernica Monastery.

sections.heading: Three Years Dead, He Became "the Most Romanian of All Our Painters"
sections.body: A retrospective mounted at Bucharest's Dalles Hall in the spring of 1965 — organised posthumously with the critic Petru Comarnescu among its champions — did what seven lifetime exhibitions and one living-room show had not: it made Țuculescu famous. [Two hundred and seventy-one works](https://www.observatorcultural.ro/articol/dincolo-de-dramatismul-naturist-al-lui-ion-tuculescu/) went up. Its own guest book split just as sharply as the one from 1956. One visitor called him ["cel mai român dintre toți pictorii noștri"](https://romanialiterara.com/2020/06/ion-tuculesc-expozitia-retrospectiva-din-1965/) — the most Romanian of all our painters. Another dismissed the show as ["gunoi,"](https://romanialiterara.com/2020/06/ion-tuculesc-expozitia-retrospectiva-din-1965/) garbage, warning that "molima decadenței în artă," the plague of decadence in art, had reached Romania. Both readings were arguing about the same body of work: the folkloric paintings, and the increasingly abstract, totemic ones that followed them, made in years when nobody in an official capacity was allowed to see them. The touring exhibitions that followed went on to [Venice, San Francisco, Washington, London, Paris and Rome](https://www.rri.ro/en/features-and-reports/rri-encyclopaedia/874917-id874917.html). Blue Totem, undated even now, belongs to that closing, unwatched decade — the one the state spent years making sure almost nobody saw.
